questions.title: Two Sum — why a hash map
questions.question: You need to find two numbers in an unsorted array that add up to a target. What data structure lets you do this in a single pass with O(n) time?
options: A hash map from value to index
A sorted copy of the array
questions.explanation: As you scan, store each value's index in a hash map and check whether target - current has already been seen. Lookups are O(1), giving one pass and O(n) total.

questions.title: Valid Parentheses — the right structure
questions.question: To check whether brackets like (), [], and {} are correctly matched and nested, which structure naturally models the 'most recently opened must close first' rule?
questions.explanation: A stack is LIFO: push each opening bracket, and on a closing bracket pop and confirm it matches. An empty stack at the end means every bracket was balanced.

questions.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
questions.question: Given daily prices, you may buy once and sell once later for maximum profit. What must you track while scanning left to right?
options: The maximum price seen so far
The minimum price so far and the best profit so far
questions.explanation: Track the lowest price seen so far as a candidate buy day; at each day compute price - minSoFar and update the best profit. One pass, O(n) time and O(1) space.

questions.title: Contains Duplicate
questions.question: What is the most time-efficient way to determine if any value appears at least twice in an array?
options: Compare every pair with nested loops
Sort the array, then compare neighbors
Insert into a hash set and check for a collision
Use binary search for each element
questions.explanation: Adding elements to a hash set and stopping the moment an insert finds an existing value is O(n) time. Sorting works but is O(n log n); nested loops are O(n^2).

questions.title: Maximum Subarray — Kadane's insight
questions.question: Kadane's algorithm finds the maximum-sum contiguous subarray. At each element, what decision does it make?
options: Whether to extend the current subarray or start fresh at this element
Whether to sort the remaining elements
Whether to remove the smallest element
Whether to split the array in half
questions.explanation: current = max(num, current + num): either extend the running subarray or restart at the current element. Track the best current seen. This is O(n).

questions.title: Binary Search — the precondition
questions.question: Binary search achieves O(log n) lookup, but only if which condition holds for the input array?
questions.explanation: Binary search relies on order: comparing the middle element tells you which half to discard. Without a sorted array that guarantee breaks and you must use linear search.

questions.title: Climbing Stairs
questions.question: You can climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. The number of distinct ways to reach step n follows which well-known sequence?
questions.explanation: ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2), because the last move is either a 1-step or a 2-step. That recurrence is exactly Fibonacci, computable in O(n) time and O(1) space.

questions.title: Invert Binary Tree
questions.question: Inverting a binary tree means mirroring it. What is the cleanest recursive step at each node?
options: Delete the node and rebuild it
Swap the node's left and right children, then recurse on both
Rotate the node to the root
questions.explanation: Swap left and right, then recursively invert each subtree. The base case is a null node. Every node is visited once, so it is O(n).
